github-copilot.title: Route and orchestrate models with GitHub Copilot Fusion
github-copilot.summary: GitHub Copilot Fusion is generally available. Instead of picking a model for each task, choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you. Copilot Fusion brings together Project HydraFusion’s multi-model…
github-copilot.html:
GitHub Copilot Fusion is generally available. Instead of picking a model for each task, choose Copilot Fusion and let Copilot intelligently route and orchestrate which models it uses for you.

Copilot Fusion brings together Project HydraFusion’s multi-model orchestration and Copilot auto model selection’s fine-tuned model selection, leveraging the benefits of both to balance performance and cost efficiency.

Since Project HydraFusion launched, we’ve improved its performance. In the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, Copilot Fusion Max scored 60, within two points of Claude Code with Opus 5.5 Max. It delivered that result at about half the average API cost per task, using about half as many tokens and taking about 40% less time per task.

Smarter choices for developers

When you select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, you aren’t selecting a specific model. You’re choosing a system that routes and orchestrates models for each task. There’s no need to switch models during a task or decide which model suits each step. For each prompt, Copilot Fusion determines which models to use and how they work together, while you choose the right level of effort.

To use it, select Copilot Fusion in the model picker, then choose the effort level.

  • Fusion Standard: Prioritizes versatile models for everyday coding.
  • Fusion High: Prioritizes capable models for challenging tasks and deeper reasoning.
  • Fusion Max: Prioritizes the most capable models for the most demanding tasks and complex reasoning.

Watch as Copilot Fusion analyzes each task and selects a model to complete it, orchestrating multiple models through the following workflows when needed.

  • Single: One model solves the task directly.
  • Cascade: An efficient model drafts a response. A quality check determines whether to accept it or escalate to a stronger model.
  • Critique: One model drafts an initial response, another model reviews it, and the original model revises.

More control for administrators

Administrators control which models Copilot Fusion can use and whether Copilot Fusion is the default.

  • Copilot Fusion only uses the models that are enabled in your enterprise and organization model policies. Enterprise administrators can view what models Copilot Fusion picks from, independently set each model’s effective policy state, and disable models for Copilot Fusion without disabling the model for everyone. See Manage availability of default models.
  • Administrators can set Copilot Fusion, at any effort level, as the default model for Copilot users with Enterprise managed settings. To configure settings, see Enterprise managed settings.

“GitHub Copilot Fusion Standard has improved token efficiency across AT&T by automatically selecting the right model for the task, reducing unnecessary spend and preserving capacity for higher-value work. Previously, developers would often choose a more powerful model for a complex task and forget to switch back for everyday activities. Copilot Fusion eliminates that friction, optimizing model selection without requiring developers to manage it themselves. We’ve also seen its decision-making improve over time, giving developers greater confidence to focus on their work while Copilot handles model selection.”
Hari Pokhrel, Principal Software Engineer, AT&T

Billing

When you use Copilot Fusion you’re billed for each model it uses, at each model’s standard rate. For a limited time, users on paid Copilot plans will receive a 30% discount on model costs when using Copilot Fusion.

Get started

Copilot Fusion is available on all Copilot plans in Visual Studio Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Copilot CLI, and JetBrains IDEs. Support for additional clients is coming soon.

Update your client to try it out. Open the model picker, select Copilot Fusion, and choose an effort level.

Note for research preview participants: if you previously enabled auto, HydraFusion, or HydraFusion Max, your selections will automatically transition to the corresponding Copilot Fusion effort levels.

To learn more, see our documentation on GitHub Copilot Fusion and share your feedback in the GitHub Community.

The post Route and orchestrate models with GitHub Copilot Fusion appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Copilot app, Universe releases
github-copilot.summary: Work doesn’t always fit in a single repository or session. A feature can span several repositories. A launch plan can pull in specs, designs, and assets without touching a repository at all. Projects in the GitHub Copilot app give that work one home, with its…
github-copilot.html:
Work doesn’t always fit in a single repository or session. A feature can span several repositories. A launch plan can pull in specs, designs, and assets without touching a repository at all. Projects in the GitHub Copilot app give that work one home, with its context, agents, and results together. Copilot coordinates the work in the background and checks in when it needs you.

Give Copilot a goal

Start a project, describe what you want to get done, and add the context Copilot needs (e.g., repositories, design mocks, Slack threads, or notes from a design meeting). Choose the models and tools for the job. Copilot runs as many agents as the work needs and brings back results (e.g., pull requests) for your review.

Use project automations for repeatable tasks, such as creating a new promo video whenever a feature lands.

For a focused task in a single repository, you can still start a session directly from that repository.

Copilot Projects are now in public preview. You can learn more in the projects documentation.

Handle the work around your code

Use context from connected tools such as Slack and Figma to research a request, draft a specification, or work through a design alongside your code.

You can also generate and edit images using natural language in chat.

Let Copilot work with your desktop apps

Ask Copilot to work through tasks in your desktop apps, such as an expense-report workflow. Computer use—in public preview on macOS and Windows—lets Copilot read app content, click controls, enter or edit text, and navigate across apps, including those without an API, command-line interface, or MCP integration.

Copilot asks for your approval before controlling an app, and your organization can disable the feature through managed settings. To get started, open Settings > Computer Use and turn on Enable Computer Use. On macOS, grant the required Accessibility and Screen Recording permissions.


For more information, see the computer use documentation.

Get started

Download or update the GitHub Copilot app and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

The post GitHub Copilot app, Universe releases appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Enterprise now includes access to GitHub Copilot
github-copilot.summary: Enterprises working with a GitHub or Microsoft account team can now get Copilot included with GitHub Enterprise for every licensed user. Previously, you had to manage two things: how many Copilot seats you were paying for and how much AI usage those users…
github-copilot.html:
Enterprises working with a GitHub or Microsoft account team can now get Copilot included with GitHub Enterprise for every licensed user. Previously, you had to manage two things: how many Copilot seats you were paying for and how much AI usage those users consumed. With Copilot included in the platform, usage against your enterprise budget is the primary thing to manage.

Self-serve availability is coming in stages, and current self-serve subscriptions are unaffected. Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise remain available.

Users in your enterprise account who do not hold a GitHub Enterprise license get the same Copilot access through Copilot Standalone, at $10 per user per month.

Copilot access through GitHub Enterprise and Copilot Standalone has the same features and models as Copilot Enterprise but does not include monthly AI credits per seat.

What you manage

AI usage is metered from the first request against your enterprise budget, using the policies, alerts, and attribution you already have. There is no included usage allowance to track or top up. To learn more, review our documentation on Copilot billing for enterprises.

  • Code completion and next edit suggestions keep working even with no budget available.
  • Copilot Chat, Copilot code review, and Copilot in the cloud require available budget to use.
  • An exhausted budget never removes access. The seat and the features that don’t need budget stay.

Availability

  • If you work with a GitHub or Microsoft account team: Available now for GitHub Enterprise Cloud. Talk to your sales team about setting up a new enterprise account on this model or transitioning an existing enterprise account.
  • If you manage your own subscription: Currently unavailable. We are opening this to self-serve customers in stages and will share dates in the coming weeks. Your current subscription is unaffected.
  • Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise: Both remain available to purchase for new and existing enterprises.

To learn more, check out our updated documentation on Copilot access.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

The post GitHub Enterprise now includes access to GitHub Copilot appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

github-copilot.title: Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app
github-copilot.summary: You can now work through your repository’s GitHub code scanning alerts without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. The new GitHub security extension, now in public preview, lets you find the alerts that matter most and ask Copilot to explain or help fix them.…
github-copilot.html:
You can now work through your repository’s GitHub code scanning alerts without leaving the GitHub Copilot app. The new GitHub security extension, now in public preview, lets you find the alerts that matter most and ask Copilot to explain or help fix them.

Until now, fixing a code scanning alert meant switching between the alert on github.com and the code in your editor. With the security extension, you can move from finding an alert to fixing it in one place.

Fix the alerts already in your code

If you already run code scanning on your repository, the security extension shows its open code scanning alerts:

  • Browse every open code scanning alert, ordered by severity, and use search and filters to narrow the list.
  • Open an alert to see its details and the affected code. You can open the full alert page on github.com when you need more context.
  • Select one or more alerts and ask Copilot to Explain or Fix them. Copilot only makes fixes in your local working copy and doesn’t commit or push anything. This way you can review and iterate on the changes in the app and push when you’re ready.
  • See linked pull requests on an alert so you know whether someone is already working on a fix.
  • Dismiss alerts you don’t plan to fix. If your organization uses delegated alert dismissal, the extension sends your dismissal for approval.

Catch new issues before you open a pull request
  • Run /security-review on your current changes and see those findings next to your existing alerts.
  • The extension tells you when your code has changed since the last review so you know when to run it again.

You can also ask Copilot about your alerts in chat. Copilot uses the security extension’s tools in the same way as any other tool, following your tool permission settings.

Get started

To install the security extension:

  • In your terminal run copilot plugin install github-security@awesome-copilot.
  • In the GitHub Copilot app, click Customize, search for github-security, then click + Install.

The extension is automatically enabled, and you can open the Security canvas from a session for your repository.

The Explain, Fix, and /security-review actions use the model you’ve selected in the app and consume AI credits in the same way as any other prompt. Browsing and dismissing alerts don’t use AI.

The security extension is in public preview on github.com and GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency. GitHub Enterprise Server isn’t supported.

  • With any Copilot plan: You can install the extension and run /security-review on your local changes. For Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise, an administrator needs to enable the GitHub Copilot app policy, and can use enterprise managed settings to control which plugins developers can install.
  • With code scanning: You can see, fix, and dismiss existing alerts for repositories where code scanning is enabled and you have permission to view the alerts. Private repositories need GitHub Code Security for this.

Learn more in the security extension documentation and join the discussion in GitHub Community.

The post Security extension for the GitHub Copilot app appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

github-copilot.title: GitHub intelligence puts your code, context, and history to work
github-copilot.summary: Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces…
github-copilot.html:
Agents should understand more than your codebase—they should understand how your team works. Your preferences, repository conventions, skills, and custom instructions guide how changes should be made, while code in related repositories can show how the pieces fit together. Without that context, agents spend time rediscovering knowledge and can miss your team’s conventions.

GitHub intelligence is the context and learning layer sourced from the graph of GitHub data. It makes this data useful to agents, helping them remember how you work, keep that guidance current, and find the code and development history relevant to the next task. The goal is for agents to build on what you and your team already know, rather than treating every session as a fresh start.

That is the advantage of building where your team’s work already lives. A repository memory can capture why an edge case matters and which test covers it. GitHub intelligence allows agents to use that context, with controls over what they can access.

Three capabilities bring this into your workflow:

  • Memory carries knowledge between sessions
  • Dreaming keeps the context current
  • Code search reaches beyond your checkout.

Availability and settings vary by capability.

Memory: Pick up where you left off

GitHub Copilot Memory is now generally available on paid Copilot plans. Copilot can remember personal preferences and repository conventions across sessions and clients. Memories can be created in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, VS Code, Copilot cloud agent, Copilot code review, Slack, Teams, and GitHub Mobile.

You can tell Copilot, Remember to start my pull request descriptions with a TL;DR, and it can reuse that preference across Copilot experiences. Repository memories can capture the right test command or how your team expects Copilot to check its work, so you spend less time repeating guidance in each session. Copilot sessions autonomously generate and curate memories, learning from every interaction.

Among the Copilot CLI sessions reviewed during the public preview where the agent used memory, 93% showed better adherence to developer preferences and 42% showed more efficient workflows attributed to the memories included in the session context.

You can interact with memories in the Copilot app, Copilot CLI, and VS Code, or manage personal memories in your Copilot settings, where you can view or delete saved preferences.

Dreaming: Continuous context improvement

Copilot dreaming, now in public preview, reflects on past work to improve future agentic sessions.

Three dream types are currently available:

  • Personal memory curation customizes Copilot to your personal preferences by updating memories based on your agent conversations.
  • Repository customization manages repository-scoped memories and proposes updates and improvements to existing skills and custom instruction files.
  • Code review customization turns recurring accepted code-review feedback into guidance for Copilot code review.

Dreaming can add, update, and remove personal and repository memories. Changes to checked-in skills and instructions are proposed in pull requests for your team to review.

Dreaming is opt-in.

  • Individual subscribers: Enable personal curation in your Copilot settings and repository dreams in each repository’s settings. See personal and repository setup.
  • Organizations and enterprises: Administrators enable dreaming through Copilot policies. Enterprise administrators can delegate that choice to organization administrators. Repository dreams cover the repositories allowed by Copilot Memory’s repository access settings. Users must also enable personal dreaming in their own Copilot settings.

Dream runs consume AI credits. See the dreaming documentation for prerequisites, setup, and costs.

Code Search: Reach beyond your checkout

Software projects rarely live in a single repository. GitHub code search helps Copilot find relevant code, configuration, schemas, and documentation across related projects and dependencies without needing a local clone. Copilot can search for exact text and symbols, match patterns with regular expressions, and narrow results by repository, path, or language. Semantic search can also find code by what it does, such as retrying a failed payment, even when you don’t know the file, function name, or repository it lives in.

For example, you’re fixing failed payments, but retry behavior spans a payments service, a shared library, and background workers. Use /research to ask Copilot, How do these components retry failed charges, and where could retries overlap? Copilot can inspect implementations and callers across those repositories to help you understand how the system fits together before changing it.

That unlocks workflows that would otherwise require you to assemble the context yourself:

  • Plan a migration: Use /research to identify implementations and callers across repositories, plan the changes each service needs, and check which projects still use the old API.
  • Investigate a bug: Trace related implementations across services and shared libraries, bring specific code references into the investigation, and use that context to propose a coordinated fix.
  • Follow organizational standards: Find existing patterns across your organization and use them to guide changes in an unfamiliar codebase.

Whether the task calls for an exact symbol, a regular expression in file contents or paths, or a natural-language description, Copilot can search across repositories in your organization to find relevant context. You spend less time cloning projects, tracking down files, and copying code into the conversation. In addition, Copilot gets the context it needs to make the right changes.

Try it today

Your team shouldn’t have to teach every agent the same lessons. GitHub intelligence helps agents carry those lessons forward, find the context they need, and put more of each session toward the work you actually want done.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

github-copilot.title: Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations
github-copilot.summary: Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together. With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Copilot runs autonomously…
github-copilot.html:
Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out, enabling teams to build and maintain AI-powered workflows together.

With Copilot Automations, you can combine prompts, triggers, and tools to design workflows around the way your team works. Copilot runs autonomously in the cloud, using only the tools you’ve allowed. For example, you could create automations to:

  • Reproduce bugs as soon as an issue is opened.
  • Capture screenshots of the changes when a pull request is marked as ready.
  • Automatically investigate production incidents as soon as they’re detected in your monitoring tool.

Until now, automations have been personal, meaning only you could see and edit them, and they used your identity and AI credits. That works well for automating your own work, like drafting your standup updates, but not for workflows your whole team relies on. Shared automations let your team build and maintain those workflows together.

How shared automations work

  • Visible to your team: Everyone with read access to the repository can see a shared automation, and anyone with write access can edit it.
  • Billed to the repository owner: AI credits are billed to the organization or user that owns the repository, rather than to the person who created the automation.
  • Act as Copilot: Actions on GitHub are attributed to Copilot, rather than to any one user.
  • Built to last: Shared automations belong to the repository, so they keep running if the person who created them leaves the team. Change history lets your team see how the tools, triggers, and prompt have evolved.

For shared automations to run in an organization-owned repository, an administrator must enable the “Allow use of Copilot cloud agent billed to the organization” policy.

Create a shared automation

When you create an automation on github.com, the GitHub Copilot app , or Visual Studio Code, choose Shared under Type. You can’t change an automation’s type after you create it. To learn more, see personal and shared automations.

Shared Copilot Automations are rolling out to users on Copilot Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise plans. Availability may vary as the rollout progresses. Once available, you can create automations in any repository where you have write access.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

The post Build shared workflows for your team with Copilot Automations appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Copilot in VS Code, Universe releases
github-copilot.summary: This year, we focused on giving you more choice in how you work with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code: which models you use, where your agents run, and how you stay involved. Keep work moving without staying at your desk or in one tool. With GitHub Copilot…
github-copilot.html:
This year, we focused on giving you more choice in how you work with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code: which models you use, where your agents run, and how you stay involved.

Keep work moving without staying at your desk or in one tool. With GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio Code, start a cloud agent session from your phone at standup, steer it from VS Code at your desk, and check on it from github.com at lunch. Session continuity lets you pick up the same session across these clients while your agent keeps working in the cloud.

Start and follow cloud sessions across Copilot clients

Hand off work without keeping your computer on. Start a cloud agent session from the Agents window in VS Code. The work runs on GitHub’s infrastructure, so closing your laptop doesn’t stop it.

Find and continue the same session in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, GitHub Mobile, github.com, or Copilot CLI. Sessions started in a Slack or Microsoft Teams DM can also be continued in these clients.


Keep agents working on your own machines

Move on to another task or project without worrying about losing your session. The new Agent Host isolates your Copilot sessions from individual VS Code windows, so work continues in the background after you close the project folder or window.

You can also run agents on a separate machine while you use your primary development machine for other work. The power and flexibility of VS Code’s Remote SSH and dev tunnels extends to the Agents window. The remote agent works with the same code, tools, and dependencies, and can keep running when you disconnect or quit VS Code locally. The remote machine and its Agent Host must remain running.

Move between the editor and Agents windows

Switch between the editor and the Agents window without starting over. Both views stay in sync with the same live Copilot session.


Control agents on your machine from your phone

Check progress, give direction, or start a new task on your development machine from GitHub Mobile. Your phone provides the controls, and the agent does the work on your development machine. To get started, open a terminal on that machine and run the VS Code CLI command code agent host --github-environment from your project folder. Keep the machine and its Agent Host running while you use it from your phone.


Get a more consistent GitHub Copilot

Get more consistent agent behavior across VS Code, Copilot CLI, and the GitHub Copilot app. The Copilot harness, built on the Microsoft Copilot SDK, is now the default for new sessions in both the editor and the Agents window.

Install GitHub Copilot CLI with VS Code

Bring Copilot to your terminal with less setup. Install GitHub Copilot CLI through the VS Code installer on Windows, when adding VS Code to your path on macOS, or by running copilot on Linux.

Compare model results

Explore different approaches to the same coding task. Run models and harnesses in parallel in the Agents window, then review their results side by side. You can ask a Judge model to recommend a solution and choose Synthesize to combine ideas from the other attempts. This is in preview.


Let your agent use your desktop apps

Give your agent tasks that need more than code or terminal commands. With computer use, Copilot can read and interact with desktop apps, including clicking controls and editing text.

On macOS or Windows, open VS Code Settings, search for chat.agentHost.computerUse.enabled, and enable it. Restart VS Code, then run /computer on in a Copilot session running on your computer.

Each application requires your approval. Computer use shares its setup with Copilot CLI and the GitHub Copilot app, so on macOS you grant the required system permissions once. Organizations can disable computer use through policy.

This is an experimental feature.


Build your own client

Bring session continuity to your own app. Build a client that connects to an Agent Host and works with the same live sessions as VS Code.

The open Agent Host Protocol (AHP) lets connected clients stay in sync and catch up after reconnecting. Run code agent host, then connect with a client library for TypeScript, Rust, Go, Kotlin, or Swift.

Discover marketplace customizations

Create, discover, and manage agent customizations from one place in VS Code. Open Customizations in the Agents window sidebar or run Chat: Open Customizations. Its “Browse” page brings together skills, MCP servers, plugins, and other customizations from available sources.

The Customization Marketplace is in preview and enabled by default. Business and Enterprise administrators need to allow Editor preview features. Learn more about the Agent Customizations editor and marketplace.

Strengthen existing plugin and marketplace controls

Make existing plugin and marketplace controls more reliable. In VS Code, administrators can use policies to require or block named plugins, add marketplaces, and restrict installation to approved sources. Enterprise-managed strict marketplace settings can also turn off built-in marketplaces. Policy-managed plugin toggles are locked in Customize > Plugins. For controls across Copilot clients, administrators can use enterprise-managed settings.

At the repository level, .github/copilot/settings.json can register plugin marketplaces and enable default plugins. These are defaults, not enforcement: contributors can turn plugins off unless enterprise policy requires them. Learn more about plugin marketplaces and workspace recommendations.

Connect services with Copilot connectors

Bring context from services such as Slack, Notion, and Microsoft Learn into agent sessions without installing or managing an MCP server. Connect once from “Browse” and reuse the connection across supported Copilot clients signed in with the same account.

Connectors are in preview, available on all Copilot plans, and work with the Copilot harness. Business and Enterprise administrators need to allow Editor preview features. Learn more about Copilot connectors in VS Code.

Learn more

Enterprises can require plugins, block plugins, and restrict installation to approved marketplaces.

As a repository maintainer, you can define a plugin marketplace and default plugins so contributors don’t have to repeat setup for each project. Contributors can turn off repository defaults where policy permits.

As an enterprise administrator, you can supply approved marketplaces and require or block plugins through managed settings. Required plugins are automatically installed and enabled, and users can’t disable them. Managed settings take precedence over repository and personal choices.

Repository defaults are available to individual Copilot users and users with Copilot Business or Copilot Enterprise.

github-copilot.title: Generate and edit images directly in Copilot
github-copilot.summary: You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your…
github-copilot.html:
You can now generate and edit images using natural language in GitHub Copilot. When you ask for an image, your selected reasoning model calls a dedicated image-generation tool powered by GPT Image 2.5 Flare, previews the result inline, and saves it to your project.

Previously, getting a visual asset while working in Copilot meant stepping away to a separate tool, describing what you needed again, generating it there, and manually bringing it back into your project. This update removes that context switch, so you can go from an idea to a usable image without breaking your flow.

  • Describe an image conversationally in any Copilot chat session, whether you’re starting a new request or in the middle of a coding task.
  • Copilot previews the generated image inline and saves it directly to your workspace.
  • Organization and enterprise owners can turn off image generation by disabling the image generation model using Copilot model policies.
  • You can opt in to a visible “Made with AI” watermark on images Copilot generates and edits. Watermarking is off by default.

To try it, open a Copilot chat in VS Code, the GitHub Copilot app, or Copilot CLI and describe the image you want.

Image generation is in public preview for Copilot Pro, Copilot Pro+, Copilot Business, and Copilot Enterprise. It’s billed separately from your chat model, based on image tokens that count toward your plan’s AI credits.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Copilot Fusion now supports selection of local models
github-copilot.summary: Today we are shipping intelligent routing for local models into experimental preview. GitHub Copilot Fusion can now choose between supported on-device models and cloud models, enabling intelligent local model routing in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app,…
github-copilot.html:
Today we are shipping intelligent routing for local models into experimental preview. GitHub Copilot Fusion can now choose between supported on-device models and cloud models, enabling intelligent local model routing in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app, and Visual Studio Code. This opt-in experimental preview lets you use your device’s compute without switching models manually for each request. For a deeper dive into this feature, see our original announcement on October 7th.

Managed download and setup on Windows

On supported Windows devices, you can download and configure MAI Code 1.1 Flash through the Windows ML provider.

  • In Copilot CLI, enable experimental mode and open /model to follow the setup prompts.
  • In the Copilot app, configure the Windows ML provider under Settings > Model providers, enable Local model auto routing under Settings > Experiments, and start a new session. Windows ML local models is enabled by default on Windows.
  • In VS Code, enable chat.copilot.localModel.enabled.

Once the model is ready, select Standard in Copilot Fusion to let Copilot choose between local and cloud models. You can also select the local model directly for your session.

Bring your own local model

The managed download experience is Windows-only, but Copilot CLI’s local Copilot Fusion routing also works with manually configured models on Windows, macOS, and Linux.

You can configure MAI Code 1.1 Flash or Qwen3.8 Flash Next through a local OpenAI-compatible server. You manage the model download and inference runtime, and your device must have sufficient resources to run it. Configure the model as a supported local-model provider, enable experimental local routing, and select Standard in Copilot Fusion to let Copilot choose between eligible local and cloud models.

This builds on the recent local-model discovery improvements in Copilot CLI. Adding or discovering a model through bring your own key (BYOK) configuration doesn’t automatically make it eligible for Copilot Fusion.

The Copilot app also supports connecting and directly selecting compatible local models through BYOK. However, its intelligent routing currently supports managed Windows ML models only.

Local inference doesn’t make your session offline. Copilot Fusion still makes routing decisions in the cloud, and local models may have different safety protections from Copilot-provided cloud models.

For setup instructions, see Adding LLM models to GitHub Copilot CLI and Adding LLM models to the GitHub Copilot app. For routing behavior, see our docs on intelligent routing to local models.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Agentic Workflows generally available
github-copilot.summary: GitHub Agentic Workflows, an open source project from GitHub Next, is now generally available. With agentic workflows, you can automate reasoning-based tasks like issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates, and test writing by using coding agents…
github-copilot.html:
GitHub Agentic Workflows, an open source project from GitHub Next, is now generally available. With agentic workflows, you can automate reasoning-based tasks like issue triage, CI failure analysis, documentation updates, and test writing by using coding agents inside GitHub Actions.

Define your automation in natural language Markdown files, and GitHub Agentic Workflows compiles them into standard Actions YAML. Because these are GitHub Actions, they reuse your existing runner groups and policy constraints. You can use GitHub Copilot or bring your own coding agent to power each workflow.

We’ve been rolling out our agentic developer workflows, and the results are measurable. One of our leads saved an estimated 29 hours a week on his development work alone. Across his team, measured velocity has more than doubled on average, and AI now authors 91% of the team’s commits. With these workflows, the team cut production errors from about 11,000 a day to under 1,000 and drove a technology migration end to end.

One workflow takes a feature from requirements to implementation with validation evidence. Others keep our frameworks current and steadily raise code quality and test coverage. Because AI drives the process to completion, our engineers can run four or five efforts in parallel and stay focused on the bigger goals.
Ben Alton – Senior manager, Strategy, Architecture & Innovation team at Accenture

Built-in safeguards

GitHub Agentic Workflows incorporates layered safeguards for your automation. Agents access GitHub content respecting the integrity filter rules, run with read-only permissions by default, and execute inside a sandboxed container behind the Agent Workflow Firewall. The outputs are validated through the safe outputs process, and a dedicated threat detection job scans all proposed changes before they are applied.

Additional capabilities for general availability

Highlights since the public preview include:

  • Actions Runner Controller (ARC) and Docker-in-Docker support: Run agentic workflows on self-hosted ARC runners with Docker-in-Docker.
  • Improved budget forecasting: gh aw forecast is no longer experimental. It now includes both threat detection credits and monthly ranges for a fuller picture of your AI credit spend.
  • New models, engine choices, and workflows: The model inventory has been refreshed, model providers can be picked per workflow, and there are new workflow templates that can be added with gh aw add-wizard.
  • Model routing: Workflows can use a model router that optimizes for task type and difficulty.
  • Improved agent isolation: Agents can run in a Cloud Hypervisor or NVX micro-VM and prevent data leaks in cross-repository workflows with enclaves.

See the GitHub Agentic Workflows release notes for the full list of changes.

Get started

Follow the quickstart guide to install the CLI extension and trigger your first workflow in minutes. Explore prebuilt workflows in GitHub Next’s agentics repository for ready-to-use examples covering triage, dependency management, code review, and reporting.

GitHub Agentic Workflows is now generally available on github.com for GitHub Free, Team, and Enterprise. Using the default GitHub Copilot CLI engine to power a workflow requires a Copilot license.

Learn more in the GitHub Agentic Workflows documentation, and join the conversation in the community discussion.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Copilot supports server-to-server authentication
github-copilot.summary: GitHub Copilot now supports server-to-server authentication for GitHub Apps installed on organizations, available in public preview. Services and agents built with the GitHub Copilot SDK can now make requests on behalf of an organization without relying on a…
github-copilot.html:
GitHub Copilot now supports server-to-server authentication for GitHub Apps installed on organizations, available in public preview. Services and agents built with the GitHub Copilot SDK can now make requests on behalf of an organization without relying on a signed-in user’s credentials. This workload-owned identity helps agents and automated services operate reliably at larger scale without tying their authentication or usage to individual users.

Developers can give a GitHub App the read-only Copilot Requests organization permission, install the app on an organization, and pass a short-lived installation access token to the Copilot SDK. Usage is attributed and billed to the organization that owns the installation. The organization’s model policies, budgets, and spending controls apply.

Organization owners can review which apps have access, identify app-attributed usage in AI usage CSV reports using the app_client_id field, and stop an app’s access by suspending or uninstalling it.

To get started, see server-to-server authentication for the GitHub Copilot SDK and managing GitHub App access to your organization’s Copilot.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Copilot assisted permissions generally available
github-copilot.summary: Assisted permissions are now generally available in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app, and Visual Studio Code. When Copilot requests permission to run a command, access a file system path, or open a URL, a large language model evaluates the request.…
github-copilot.html:
Assisted permissions are now generally available in GitHub Copilot CLI, GitHub Copilot app, and Visual Studio Code.

When Copilot requests permission to run a command, access a file system path, or open a URL, a large language model evaluates the request. Requests classified as clearly safe automatically proceed. Other requests require your approval.

GitHub Copilot CLI

Run /permissions, then select assisted.

GitHub Copilot app

Open the mode picker, click Tool permissions, then select Assisted.

Visual Studio Code

Open the permissions picker, then select Assisted permissions.

Enterprise controls

If you’re an enterprise administrator, you can use enterprise-managed settings to block Allow All while keeping Assisted available or disable Assisted separately.

You can also choose the default permission mode for new sessions. Developers can still select another mode permitted by policy. If the default is unavailable or prohibited by policy, the session starts with manual approval.

For details about how assisted permissions evaluate requests and when approval is required, see Allowing safe commands to run without manual approval.

github-copilot.html:

In early testing, GPT-6.1 Terra solved noticeably more terminal and C# coding tasks than GPT-5.6 Terra. It works in focused, consolidated steps on well-scoped tasks.

This model is billed at provider list pricing under usage-based billing. See Models and pricing for GitHub Copilot for details.

  • GitHub Mobile on iOS and Android

  • Xcode

Copilot Enterprise and Copilot Business plan administrators can manage access to GPT-6.1 Terra through the model policy in Copilot settings. github-copilot.title: Usage metrics API adds usage from tools like OpenCode
github-copilot.summary: The Copilot usage metrics API now reports model usage from more of the tools your developers use with Copilot, including tools like OpenCode that weren’t previously captured in your reports. A new totals_by_client array is available in the enterprise,…
github-copilot.html:
The Copilot usage metrics API now reports model usage from more of the tools your developers use with Copilot, including tools like OpenCode that weren’t previously captured in your reports. A new totals_by_client array is available in the enterprise, organization, enterprise-user, and organization-user 1-day and 28-day reports.

What’s new

Each totals_by_client entry represents one client and includes:

  • client: The tool that sent the requests, such as opencode, claude_code, codex, zed, copilot_cli, github_app, cloud_agent, code_review, vscode, or jetbrains. Unrecognized clients are grouped under other.
  • request_count: The number of successful model requests from the client.
  • session_count: The number of distinct sessions from the client.
  • token_usage: Prompt tokens, output tokens, and average tokens per request.
  • totals_by_model: The same request and token metrics broken down by model, with a model_selection_mode that shows whether the model was requested directly (user_selected), chosen by auto (auto), or chosen by the product (product_selected). Selection modes that aren’t reported individually yet appear as other, and values that can’t be normalized appear as unknown.
Why this matters

More developers now use Copilot as the model provider behind tools outside the IDE. Because those tools often don’t send editor telemetry, their usage was missing from totals_by_ide and hard to account for. Counting requests on the server closes that gap, so you can see which tools drive Copilot usage, compare request and token volume across them, and base tool support and governance decisions on real usage.

This is different from agent app activity, which counts jobs started by agent apps such as Claude and Codex on GitHub. totals_by_client measures model traffic, meaning requests and tokens, from any tool that uses Copilot.

Important notes
  • Scope: Enterprise, organization, enterprise-user, and organization-user reports, in both 1-day and 28-day versions. In the aggregated 28-day reports, totals_by_client appears in each day_totals entry.
  • Access: Available to enterprise owners and billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the View Copilot Metrics permission. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.
  • Copilot code review and Copilot cloud agent: Requests from these clients report product_selected because the product chooses the model. Copilot code review models are reported as unknown.
  • Request counts: request_count counts model calls, not prompts. One prompt can trigger several model calls, so don’t compare this field directly with prompt or interaction counts.
  • Client identification: Clients are identified by the integration ID they send with each request. Treat client as a best-effort grouping, not a verified identity.
  • Backward compatibility: This change is additive. Existing fields are unchanged, and totals_by_client is an empty array when there is no usage to report.

Visit the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.

The post Usage metrics API adds usage from tools like OpenCode appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

github-copilot.title: GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio — September update
github-copilot.summary: September 2026 brought deeper visibility into your work: explore pull requests without leaving chat, bring the AI model your team trusts, and fix vulnerable packages the moment Visual Studio flags them. Highlights Here’s what’s new with GitHub Copilot in…
github-copilot.html:
September 2026 brought deeper visibility into your work: explore pull requests without leaving chat, bring the AI model your team trusts, and fix vulnerable packages the moment Visual Studio flags them.

Highlights

Here’s what’s new with GitHub Copilot in Visual Studio 2026. Check the Insiders channel for the latest:

  • Explore pull requests with the Git agent: The Git agent can now explore a pull request for you. Open GitHub Copilot Chat, select the Git agent, and attach a pull request as context from the Git Repository window to get a summary with navigable links to the underlying comments and files. This functionality requires connecting your Git provider’s MCP servers; GitHub and Azure DevOps are both supported.
  • Updates to Bring Your Own Model (BYOM): BYOM is available in preview and lets you use the models your team prefers, through GitHub Copilot or your own model deployments, whether or not you’re signed in to GitHub. This feature is on by default across the Community, Professional, and Enterprise editions. Breaking change: BYOM now requires the new Agent (Preview), built on the GitHub Copilot SDK-powered harness. The previous Ask and Agent modes no longer support BYOM, and you’ll need to re-add previously configured Ollama models after updating. Supported providers include Microsoft Foundry, OpenAI, Anthropic, and Ollama.
  • Fix NuGet Vulnerabilities from the Error List: NuGet Audit warnings in the Error List now include a fixer action that opens GitHub Copilot Chat in agent mode and asks Copilot to fix the vulnerable packages using the NuGet MCP server. This functionality requires signing in to GitHub Copilot and enabling the NuGet MCP server from the Copilot Chat tools menu.

This update is available to users on all GitHub Copilot plans, including Copilot Free, Student, Pro, Pro+, Max, Business, and Enterprise.

Download Visual Studio 2026 to experience all the new Copilot features today. To learn more about what’s new, check out the Visual Studio blog and release notes.

github-copilot.title: Custom skills, agents, and MCP servers in usage metrics API
github-copilot.summary: Copilot usage metrics now show the names of the skills, custom agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, slash commands, and plugins that your organization creates, instead of grouping them under other or custom. This builds on the agentic CLI…
github-copilot.html:
Copilot usage metrics now show the names of the skills, custom agents, Model Context Protocol (MCP) servers, slash commands, and plugins that your organization creates, instead of grouping them under other or custom. This builds on the agentic CLI customization metrics released in September.

What’s new

  • Named entries: In enterprise and organization reports, including per-user 1-day and 28-day reports, aggregated 1-day reports, and day_totals in aggregated 28-day reports, the totals_by_skill, totals_by_custom_agent, totals_by_mcp, totals_by_slash_cmd, and totals_by_plugin arrays now show the configured name of a customer-defined item instead of other or custom.
  • More entries: Each totals_by_* list now includes up to 25 entries per record, up from five, so you can see more of the long tail of customizations your developers use. Any remaining activity is combined into a trailing other entry.
  • Unchanged counts: interaction_count and the distinct_*_use_count fields are calculated the same way as before.

Why this matters

The customizations that matter most to an organization are often the ones its own teams build. Administrators can now see which internal skills, custom agents, and MCP servers developers actually use, track adoption after rolling out a new one, and focus enablement where it is needed.

Important notes

  • Coverage: Names are reported from Copilot CLI (interactive sessions and prompt mode), the GitHub Copilot app, clients built on the Copilot SDK (e.g., VS Code and JetBrains IDEs), and Agent Client Protocol (ACP) integrations. Prompt mode, the app, and ACP integrations require Copilot CLI 1.0.97 or later. Copilot SDK clients require SDK v1.0.21 or later. IDE integrations that aren’t built on the Copilot SDK don’t report names.
  • Configured names: Names are reported as they are configured, trimmed and limited to 128 characters. Names that look like file paths stay grouped under other or custom. Review names before sharing reports outside your organization.
  • Accuracy: These metrics come from client telemetry and can undercount activity, for example when clients are outdated or telemetry is blocked. Use them to understand trends and adoption rather than for exact accounting.
  • History: Names appear starting with report days processed after this release. Earlier days still show other or custom.
  • Access: Reports are available to enterprise owners and billing managers, organization owners, and anyone with a custom organization or enterprise role that grants the “View Copilot Metrics” permission. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.

Visit the Copilot usage metrics API documentation to get started.

github-copilot.title: Global default for Copilot features generally available
github-copilot.summary: In September, we announced a global default policy for generally available GitHub Copilot features and supported client capabilities on Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise plans. Starting today, we’re gradually rolling out enforcement of the policy through…
github-copilot.html:
In September, we announced a global default policy for generally available GitHub Copilot features and supported client capabilities on Copilot Business and Copilot Enterprise plans. Starting today, we’re gradually rolling out enforcement of the policy through October 26, so it may take effect at different times for different enterprises and organizations. Eligible features left unconfigured will be set according to the global policy. Administrators can still make explicit choices for individual features at any time.

The policy applies to eligible settings on “Features & clients” and “MCP servers in Copilot”. You can review your setting under AI Controls → Copilot → Default policy for new features. For eligibility and exceptions, see the documentation on default availability.

What’s changing

Once the policy takes effect for your enterprise or organization:

  • Eligible generally available features and capabilities left Unconfigured will be set according to the selected global default of Enabled, Disabled, or Let organizations decide. This is a one-time change. Subsequent changes to the default policy won’t change feature policies that are already set.
  • Explicit choices are preserved. If you’ve enabled or disabled an individual feature, the rollout won’t change that setting.
  • Preview features remain opt-in. If you opted into a preview that later becomes generally available, your choice will be preserved. Otherwise, the default policy will apply when it becomes eligible.

Join the discussion within GitHub Community.

github-copilot.title: Industry comparisons in the Copilot impact dashboard
github-copilot.summary: The Copilot impact dashboard now includes an “Industry comparison” section. Enterprises, and organizations that aren’t owned by an enterprise, can compare their Copilot agentic adoption and leverage with aggregated benchmarks from participating peers.…
github-copilot.html:
The Copilot impact dashboard now includes an “Industry comparison” section. Enterprises, and organizations that aren’t owned by an enterprise, can compare their Copilot agentic adoption and leverage with aggregated benchmarks from participating peers. Participation is opt-in and disabled by default.

What’s new

  • Agentic adoption and leverage benchmarks — See the percentage of your users who are agent-first or multi-agent, and how the pull request merge rate of agentic users compares with nonagentic users. Once enough businesses have opted in, each score is ranked against the peer median for the 28-day reporting period and against the top decile as the peer group grows.
  • Peer groups by company size and industry — Choose a company size (e.g., 1–999, 1,000–4,999, or 5,000+ employees) and one of ten industries, then switch between your industry and all industries. If your industry’s peer group is too small, the comparison widens to all industries for your company size, and the dashboard labels the peer group it used.
  • Copilot metrics industry comparison policy — Opt in from the dashboard or centrally from your enterprise or organization Copilot policies. Both places use the same policy, so turning it off in either place stops both contributing data and seeing comparisons.

Why this matters

Enterprise leaders can measure their own Copilot adoption, but until now they couldn’t tell whether it was leading or lagging comparable businesses. Industry comparisons add the peer context needed to set realistic goals, identify adoption gaps, and communicate progress.

Important notes

  • Rankings appear only after enough businesses have opted in to form a peer group. Especially soon after launch, you might see only the median, a broader peer group than you selected, or no ranking until more peers join. Rankings also aren’t shown when your own score can’t be calculated such as when all your users are already agent-first or multi-agent, leaving no nonagentic baseline for leverage.
  • Comparisons refresh daily. When you opt out, comparisons stop appearing right away and your data is excluded starting with the next daily update. Aggregated benchmarks contain no identifying data and are deleted after 30 days.
  • On GitHub Enterprise Cloud with data residency, you’re compared only with participants in the same region. Data is never combined across regions.
  • Organizations owned by an enterprise participate through their enterprise, and enterprises used only to assign Copilot Business licenses can’t participate. Enterprise owners, and owners of organizations that aren’t owned by an enterprise, can opt in and set the peer group. Anyone who can view the Copilot impact dashboard can see the results. The Copilot usage metrics policy must be enabled.
  • Industry comparisons appear only in the dashboard. They aren’t included in the Copilot usage metrics API, NDJSON exports, or downloads.

Visit the Copilot impact dashboard documentation to get started.

The post Industry comparisons in the Copilot impact dashboard appeared first on The GitHub Blog.

  • Fixed the Read tool sometimes failing on PDF pages with "pdftoppm failed: Could not write image" when the clean-up of old session files ran at the same time
  • Fixed the spinner, OpenTelemetry effort values and transcripts naming a newly picked effort level during a task before the model applied it; they now show the level in force

  • Fixed some sessions showing as waiting on you when the last message only mentioned items waiting on you mid-sentence
  • Fixed agent view restoring input text on the next launch after it was cleared with Ctrl+C just before exiting
  • Fixed agent view reopening in shell mode after exiting with Ctrl+D from an empty ! input
  • Fixed vim mode d, c and y with a gj or gk count larger than the lines left deleting or copying text; like Vim, they now only move the cursor
  • Fixed /verify showing a long description meant for Claude in /help and the / command menu instead of a short one
  • Improved the prompt's effort indicator: a change made mid-task now says it may wait for your next message, and the note clears when it no longer applies
  • Improved WebFetch errors in cloud sessions: a host that does not resolve is now explained as possibly outside the allowed network domains, so Claude names the host to allow
  • Changed Bedrock, Vertex, Foundry and Mantle to use the shorter system prompt for model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names and inference profile ARNs, even when they front Sonnet or Haiku; set CLAUDE_CODE_SIMPLE_SYSTEM_PROMPT=0 to keep the full prompt
  • Changed automatic model switches after a flagged message to also cover model names Claude Code doesn't recognize, such as custom deployment names; set CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_REFUSAL_FALLBACK=1 to turn them off
  • Changed usage limit messages to call the 5-hour window the "5-hour limit" instead of the "session limit"
  • Changed cloud sessions started from the CLI to get their names and branch names from the server
  • Changed prompt and agent hooks to run at most 24 at a time per session, sub-agents included, plus at most 12 that have waited longer than their event's timeout; a timeout under 1 second now counts as 1 second
  • Changed a subagent's autoCompactWindow to lower the window set by CLAUDE_CODE_AUTO_COMPACT_WINDOW, where it had no effect before; it still never raises that window
  • Changed OpenTelemetry mcp_server.name to report the real name of fixed-URL remote MCP servers declared by plugins from the official Anthropic marketplace, instead of custom
  • Changed Claude Code to stop sending the claude_code.safety_event OpenTelemetry event
  • [VSCode] Fixed sessions ending on a bare exit code when your organization's settings couldn't be loaded or were refused at startup; the tab now says why and offers Retry or Sign in again
  • [VSCode] Changed usage limit resets to show a clock time ("Resets at 3:10 PM") and to say "5-hour limit"
  • [Cloud sessions] Added an effort level to the model picker when you create or edit a routine that runs in the cloud
  • [Cloud sessions] Added a Bash editor with colors, line numbers and a Copy button to the setup script box in cloud environment settings
  • [Cloud sessions] Improved the step shown when Claude adds a repository to a cloud session: opening it now shows a short table of what happened instead of raw JSON
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed resending an unchanged message after a failed send in a cloud session sometimes running it twice
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed a failed cloud environment creation showing its error only as a toast outside the open dialog; it now appears inside the dialog
  • [Cloud sessions] Fixed Edit in a routine's menu on the Routines page going to the routine's page without opening its edit dialog
  • [Remote Control] Fixed an unarchived Remote Control session showing as working until a computer reconnected; it now shows as idle
  • [Claude Tag] Improved Claude Tag's retry notice in Slack to name the model in use, or say rate limits were hit, instead of a generic API error
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed a Claude Tag channel's on/off switch and agent settings falling back to workspace defaults when an older private Slack channel goes public and gets a new ID
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack not replying in channels whose environment has network access set to None
  • [Claude Tag] Fixed Claude in Slack sometimes posting a file in the wrong thread when it was answering in another thread of the same channel
  • [Code Review] Fixed Code Review reviewing an outdated commit, or none at all, when GitHub delivered a push event late; it now reviews the pull request's current commit

claude-code.title: Claude Code v2.1.311
claude-code.summary: What's changed Added --hold-idle-file and --max-hold-min to self-hosted-runner, to keep an idle session while your host reports processes it left running Added a tip for the Explanatory output style, shown when you ask Claude for explanations Fixed long…
claude-code.html:
What's changed

  • Added --hold-idle-file and --max-hold-min to self-hosted-runner, to keep an idle session while your host reports processes it left running
  • Added a tip for the Explanatory output style, shown when you ask Claude for explanations
  • Fixed long freezes at startup and after reading or editing files when a CLAUDE.md file holds a very long list item
  • Fixed interrupting Claude not taking effect until a timeout while an MCP server had not answered a resource read or a skill was still downloading
  • Fixed standard-context sessions stopping with "Usage credits required for 1M context" when a request ran over 200K tokens; Claude Code now compacts the conversation and continues
  • Fixed Write and Edit stalling for up to 5 seconds after they ran, and reporting 0 lines changed, when changing thousands of lines in a file
  • Fixed subagents being unable to use MCP tools from servers that finish connecting after the subagent starts
  • Fixed Claude seeing stale MEMORY.md and CLAUDE.md content right after automatic compaction when those files were edited earlier in the session
  • Fixed claude -p and SDK sessions saving transcript messages out of order or keeping messages that were taken back
  • Fixed SubagentStop hooks running about twice a minute for each running subagent instead of once when it finishes
  • Fixed the @ file picker ignoring .ignore/.rgignore negation rules that re-include git-ignored files
  • Fixed a subagent's isolated worktree being removed while a background subagent it started was still working in it
  • Fixed background agents in auto mode that wait on their own shells starting a new main conversation turn on every wake
  • Fixed the Bash tool description claiming the working directory always persists between calls
  • Fixed the environment block naming a shell commands don't run in, such as fish when the Bash tool uses zsh
  • Fixed claude mcp add, claude mcp remove and /mcp naming the current folder instead of the project entry in ~/.claude.json that holds a local-scope server when run below a repository root
  • Fixed claude mcp list and claude mcp get showing the error code twice on failed-connection lines (for example ENOENT: ENOENT: …)
  • Fixed Remote Control sessions staying on "Connecting" for about two minutes when a network proxy blocks a startup request
  • Fixed messages that Claude sends to a cloud or Remote Control session appearing as your own message in the Claude mobile apps
  • Fixed Claude not being told the cause when a file attached to a message sent over Remote Control or to a cloud session could not be saved because the disk was full, or that a message's attachments past the first 20 were left out
  • Fixed WebFetch and WebSearch hanging on a stalled response in Cowork cloud sessions; an unfinished request now fails after 300 seconds
  • Fixed a background session that crashed between turns not being restarted while it was attached, pinned, or had a scheduled task or wake-up set
  • Fixed the "background service did not respond" error suggesting the disabled claude daemon restart; it now suggests claude daemon stop --any and says it ends background sessions
  • Fixed claude respawn <id> starting the background service before reporting that no background session matches the id
  • Fixed /effort not warning about a prompt cache miss in plan mode when the plan model differs from the session model
  • Fixed /ide saying the VS Code extension was installed before the install finished or when it failed
  • Fixed the Write tool's file preview skipping rows and miscounting hidden lines when a line is wider than the terminal
  • Fixed ↑ in an agent's chat tab recalling a message that was still waiting to be delivered, so resending it sent a second copy
  • Fixed Cowork cloud sessions losing their connectors and most tools after a restart when a plugin or your settings named an agent; Cowork cloud sessions now ignore that setting
  • Fixed agent teams sessions showing an empty task list when coming back with --resume, --continue, /resume or --session-id, including after /clear or a crash, and /branch writing to the original session's list
  • Fixed pasting text that mentions an image file, such as ! open /tmp/shot.png or /review look at /tmp/shot.png, attaching the image and dropping its path from the prompt
  • Fixed the feedback draft card showing its 1/2/0 and Esc shortcuts while the prompt has text, when those keys act on the prompt instead of the card
  • Fixed a lone backslash in quotes or brackets, like "\" or (\), disappearing from Claude's responses
  • Fixed agent teammates compacting their history when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed the rewind menu offering "Summarize from here" and "Summarize up to here" when DISABLE_COMPACT is set
  • Fixed a finished /code-review, or another skill that runs in a sub-agent, running a second time when a cloud or background session restarts
  • Fixed long hidden thinking being cut off as idle on Google Vertex AI, Microsoft Foundry and Claude Platform on AWS, where the endpoint sends thinking progress updates
  • Fixed /ide saying it had installed the JetBrains plugin when nothing was installed
  • Fixed Claude Pro and Max subscribers being told to ask their admin when their subscription can't be used; the message now points to billing settings
  • Fixed the diff pane opening by itself after an edit in wide fullscreen terminals when it had nothing to show
  • Fixed /mcp showing a remote server as failed after "Clear authentication" when the server works without sign-in
  • Fixed /mcp showing "authenticated" for a remote server that Claude Code sends no credentials to
  • Fixed a --plugin-dir folder of plugins loading as one plugin when an empty .mcp.json was at its top
  • Fixed /usage never showing large prompt-cache misses under "What's contributing to your limits usage?"
  • Fixed status line links staying plain text in background sessions after you open them from a terminal that supports links
  • Fixed the /rewind confirmation saying the conversation "will be forked" when the later messages are removed from the conversation
  • Fixed the /rewind warning that wrongly said manual and Bash edits are never affected by a code restore
  • Fixed plan approval in screen reader mode sending feedback you had dismissed with Escape
  • Fixed Claude Code retrying requests the API marked not to retry, which could hold a turn for minutes or, in unattended retry mode (CLAUDE_CODE_RETRY_WATCHDOG), indefinitely
  • Linux: Fixed sandboxed Bash commands failing with bwrap: Can't create file when a --plugin-dir folder was also an added directory and permissions.blockReadsOutsideWorkingDirectories was on
  • Self-hosted runner: Fixed a session failing to start when a rate limit (HTTP 429, or a git wrapper that exits 75) blocks an added read-only repository; it now starts without that repository
  • Improved startup time for Pro and Max accounts by skipping two network requests on launches within an hour of the last check
  • Improved /teleport and claude --teleport to warn when a compacted cloud session loads from its last compaction, so the messages it summarized aren't in the local copy
  • Improved the messages shown when a background session's process exits: they no longer promise a restart that isn't coming, and they say how to resume the session
  • Improved artifacts with several views: Claude now routes each view on the link's #name and no longer says the address bar stays the same as you switch views
  • Improved shell commands that reach their timeout: the result now shows the output so far and says the command is still running in the background
  • Improved compaction: when the model's reply has no summary in it, Claude Code now usually asks for the summary once more before it replaces the conversation
  • Improved the Artifact tool's choice between a page and a document: explainers and visual or interactive work become artifact pages; documents are for writing people keep editing or pass around
